125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: \## 2. [Content Section]
161: 
162: [The actual template/checklist/snippet content]
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## N. Related Resources (optional, if present must be last)
167: 
168: [Links to related files]
169: 
170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```
216: 
217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |

305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343:

346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:
392: ```
393: Document type?
394: ├─> SKILL.md             → MUST have frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, version)
395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```
402: 
403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
414: ```python
415: def validate_document(doc, doc_type):
416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:
423:         if section not in doc.sections:
424:             errors.append(f"Missing required section: {section}")
425: 
426:     # Verify section ordering
427:     expected_order = get_section_order(doc_type)
428:     actual_order = [s.name for s in doc.sections]
429:     if actual_order != expected_order:
430:         errors.append(f"Section order incorrect. Expected: {expected_order}")
431: 
432:     # Validate frontmatter
433:     if doc.has_frontmatter:
434:         frontmatter_errors = validate_frontmatter(doc.frontmatter, doc_type)
435:         errors.extend(frontmatter_errors)
436: 
437:     return errors
438: ```

442: ## 7. WORKFLOW PATTERNS
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Show how to represent multi-step workflows using YAML structures.
445: 
446: ### YAML Pipeline: Document Creation Workflow
447: 
448: **Before (Markdown List)**:
449: ```markdown
450: 1. Analyze the request and determine document type
451: 2. Select appropriate template
452: 3. Populate template with content
453: 4. Validate structure and content
454: 5. Apply formatting standards
455: 6. Run quality checks
456: ```
457: 
458: **After (YAML Pipeline)**:
459: ```yaml
460: document_creation_workflow:
461:   phase_1_analysis:
462:     action: "Analyze request and determine document type"
463:     output: "Document type classification"
464:     validation: "Type must be one of: SKILL, Command, Knowledge, Spec, README"
465: 
466:   phase_2_template_selection:
467:     action: "Select appropriate template based on document type"
468:     output: "Template file path"
469:     depends_on: "phase_1_analysis"
470: 
471:   phase_3_population:
472:     action: "Populate template with user-provided content"
473:     output: "Draft document with filled sections"
474:     depends_on: "phase_2_template_selection"
475: 
476:   phase_4_validation:
477:     action: "Validate structure, frontmatter, section ordering"
478:     output: "Validation report (errors/warnings)"
479:     depends_on: "phase_3_population"
480: 
481:   phase_5_formatting:
482:     action: "Apply code standards (spacing, headers)"
483:     output: "Formatted document"
484:     depends_on: "phase_4_validation"
485: 
486:   phase_6_quality_check:
487:     action: "Review checklist + run AI quality evaluation"
488:     output: "Quality notes and improvement recommendations"
489:     depends_on: "phase_5_formatting"
490: ```
491: 
492: ### YAML Configuration: Feature Flags
493: 
494: **Before (Markdown Table)**:
495: ```markdown
496: | Feature           | Default | Description                         |
497: | ----------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
498: | strict_validation | true    | Enforce all validation rules        |
499: | auto_fix          | false   | Automatically fix formatting issues |
500: | frontmatter_check | true    | Validate frontmatter per document type |
501: ```
502: 
503: **After (YAML Configuration)**:
504: ```yaml
505: feature_flags:
506:   strict_validation:
507:     default: true
508:     description: "Enforce all validation rules without warnings"
509:     values: [true, false]
510: 
511:   auto_fix:
512:     default: false
513:     description: "Automatically fix formatting issues during validation"
514:     values: [true, false]
515:     warning: "Use with caution - may change document semantics"
516: 
517:   frontmatter_check:
518:     default: true
519:     description: "Validate frontmatter fields per document type"
520:     values: [true, false]
521:     enforcement_level: "error"
522: ```
523: 
524: ### YAML Workflow: Multi-Branch Decision Process
525: 
526: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
527: ```markdown
528: The system should detect when to generate variants:
529: - If user explicitly requests options (shows me options, variations, different approaches)
530: - If complexity is high (7+) and uncertainty signals are present (not sure, what would work)
531: - Otherwise, generate single solution
532: 
533: Variant count depends on complexity:
534: - Simple: 2-3 variants
535: - Standard: 3-5 variants
536: - Complex: 5-10 variants
537: ```
538: 
539: **After (YAML Multi-Branch)**:
540: ```yaml
541: variant_generation_logic:
542:   triggers:
543:     explicit:
544:       keywords: ["show me options", "variations", "different approaches", "multiple designs"]
545:       action: "Generate variants immediately"
546:       priority: "high"
547: 
548:     implicit:
549:       conditions:
550:         - "complexity >= 7"
551:         - "uncertainty_signals present"
552:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work", "best approach"]
553:       action: "Generate variants with uncertainty disclaimer"
554:       priority: "medium"
555: 
556:     default:
557:       action: "Generate single optimal solution"
558:       priority: "low"
559: 
560:   variant_count_guidelines:
561:     simple:
562:       complexity_range: [1, 3]
563:       variant_count: "2-3"
564: 
565:     standard:
566:       complexity_range: [4, 6]
567:       variant_count: "3-5"
568: 
569:     complex:
570:       complexity_range: [7, 10]
571:       variant_count: "5-10"
572: 
573:     user_specified:
574:       action: "Honor user's requested count"
575:       override: true
576: ```

675: ## 9. TEMPLATE GUIDELINES
676: 
677: ### Naming Conventions
678: 
679: **File Names** (kebab-case required):
680: - Format: `[topic]-[type].md`
681: - Use hyphens, not underscores
682: - Lowercase only
683: - Descriptive and specific
684: - Examples:
685:   - ✅ `frontmatter-templates.md`
686:   - ✅ `validation-reference.md`
687:   - ✅ `config-examples.yaml`
688:   - ✅ `packaging-guide.md`
689:   - ❌ `templates.md` (too generic)
690:   - ❌ `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (wrong case)
691:   - ❌ `frontmatter_templates.md` (underscores are not canonical)
692: 
693: **Type-Specific Patterns**:
694: 
695: | Asset Type | Naming Pattern           | Kebab-case Examples          |
696: | ---------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
697: | Template   | `[content]-templates.md` | `frontmatter-templates.md`   |
698: | Reference  | `[topic]-reference.md`   | `emoji-reference.md`         |
699: | Example    | `[topic]-examples.md`    | `optimization-examples.md`   |
700: | Guide      | `[process]-guide.md`     | `packaging-guide.md`         |
701: | Checklist  | `[topic]-checklist.md`   | `validation-checklist.md`    |
702: 
703: **Section Names**:
704: - Use title case
705: - Be descriptive but concise
706: - Number if sequential: `1. Template Name`
707: 
708: ### Content Organization
709: 
710: **Progressive Disclosure**:
711: 1. **Introduction**: What this is, why it exists (1-2 sentences)
712: 2. **Sections**: Each covers one topic completely
713: 3. **Examples**: Show, don't just tell
714: 4. **Quick Reference**: Summary at end (optional)
715: 
716: **Section Structure**:
717: - **Purpose**: Why this section exists
718: - **Guidelines**: How to use the content
719: - **Template**: Copy-paste starting point
720: - **Example**: Complete working example
721: 
722: ### Formatting Standards
723: 
724: **Code Blocks**:
725: - Always specify language: ` ```yaml `, ` ```markdown `, ` ```bash `
726: - Include comments explaining non-obvious parts
727: - Show complete, runnable examples
728: - Use placeholder values that are obviously placeholders
729: 
730: **Placeholders**:
731: - Format: `[descriptive-name]` or `your-value-here`
732: - Examples:
733:   - ✅ `[skill-name]`, `[feature-description]`, `your-project-name`
734:   - ❌ `xxx`, `placeholder`, `FIXME`
735: 
736: **Lists**:
737: - Use `-` for unordered lists
738: - Use `1.` for ordered lists
739: - Nested lists indent by 2 spaces
740: - Keep items parallel in structure
741: 
742: **Tables**:
743: - Include header row
744: - Align consistently (usually left-aligned)
745: - Keep rows concise (1-2 lines)
746: - Use for comparisons or reference data
747: 
748: ### Writing Style
749: 
750: **Clarity**:
751: - Write for someone unfamiliar with your skill
752: - Define domain-specific terms on first use
753: - Use active voice: "Create the file" not "The file should be created"
754: - Be concise but complete
755: 
756: **Examples**:
757: - Every template should have a complete example
758: - Show real-world usage, not toy examples
759: - Include common variations
760: - Annotate non-obvious parts
761: 
762: **Consistency**:
763: - Use same terminology throughout
764: - Follow patterns from other assets in the skill
765: - Match style of SKILL.md
766: - Use consistent formatting

771:

773: 
774: ```markdown

778: □ Numbered sections

780:

14: # Skill Asset File Templates - Creation Guidelines
15: 
16: Templates and guidelines for creating asset files in AI agent skills.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### Location & Naming
21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`
23: 
24: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with the appropriate extension
25: 
26: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
27: |---------------|-----------------|
28: | `frontmatter-templates.md` | `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (PascalCase) |
29: | `config-examples.yaml` | `config_examples.yaml` (snake_case) |
30: | `validation-checklist.md` | `ValidationChecklist.MD` (wrong case) |
31: | `emoji-reference.md` | `emojiReference.md` (camelCase) |
32: 
33: ### When to Create Assets
34: 
35: **Create an asset file when:**
36: - Templates users apply repeatedly
37: - Reference data >50 lines and self-contained
38: - Multiple examples of same pattern exist
39: - Lookup tables or decision matrices needed
40: - Template variations for different scenarios
41: 
42: **Keep in SKILL.md when:**
43: - Content <30 lines
44: - Tightly coupled to workflow logic
45: - Needs to be visible immediately (not progressive disclosure)
46: - Part of core instructions (RULES, WORKFLOW sections)
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 2. ASSET FILE TYPES
51: 
52: ### Template Files
53: **Purpose**: Provide copy-paste starting points for common tasks
54: 
55: **Naming**: `[content-type]-templates.md`
56: - Example: `frontmatter-templates.md`, `structure-templates.md`
57: 
58: **Structure**:
59: - One template per section
60: - Include field descriptions
61: - Show complete examples
62: - Explain when to use each template
63: 
64: **Use cases**:
65: - Document templates (SKILL.md, commands, knowledge files)
66: - Configuration templates (YAML, JSON)
67: - Code templates (functions, classes, modules)
68: 
69: ### Reference Files
70: **Purpose**: Provide lookup tables, decision trees, or reference data
71: 
72: **Naming**: `[topic]-reference.md`
73: - Example: `emoji-reference.md`, `validation-reference.md`
74: 
75: **Structure**:
76: - Tables or lists for quick lookup
77: - Decision matrices
78: - Classification systems
79: - Standards and conventions
80: 
81: **Use cases**:
82: - Emoji selection guides
83: - File type classifications
84: - Validation rule sets
85: - Naming conventions
86: 
87: ### Example Files
88: **Purpose**: Show working examples of skill outputs
89: 
90: **Naming**: `[topic]-examples.md`
91: - Example: `optimization-examples.md`, `skill-examples.md`
92: 
93: **Structure**:
94: - Before/after comparisons
95: - Annotated examples
96: - Multiple variations

125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: \## 2. [Content Section]
161: 
162: [The actual template/checklist/snippet content]
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## N. Related Resources (optional, if present must be last)
167: 
168: [Links to related files]
169: 
170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```

219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |

305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343: 
344: ---
345: 
346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:
392: ```
393: Document type?
394: ├─> SKILL.md             → MUST have frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, version)
395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```
402: 
403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
414: ```python
415: def validate_document(doc, doc_type):
416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:
423:         if section not in doc.sections:
424:             errors.append(f"Missing required section: {section}")
425: 
426:     # Verify section ordering
427:     expected_order = get_section_order(doc_type)
428:     actual_order = [s.name for s in doc.sections]
429:     if actual_order != expected_order:
430:         errors.append(f"Section order incorrect. Expected: {expected_order}")
431: 
432:     # Validate frontmatter
433:     if doc.has_frontmatter:
434:         frontmatter_errors = validate_frontmatter(doc.frontmatter, doc_type)
435:         errors.extend(frontmatter_errors)
436: 
437:     return errors
438: ```
439: 
440: ---
441: 
442: ## 7. WORKFLOW PATTERNS
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Show how to represent multi-step workflows using YAML structures.
445: 
446: ### YAML Pipeline: Document Creation Workflow
447: 
448: **Before (Markdown List)**:
449: ```markdown
450: 1. Analyze the request and determine document type
451: 2. Select appropriate template
452: 3. Populate template with content
453: 4. Validate structure and content
454: 5. Apply formatting standards
455: 6. Run quality checks
456: ```
457: 
458: **After (YAML Pipeline)**:
459: ```yaml
460: document_creation_workflow:
461:   phase_1_analysis:
462:     action: "Analyze request and determine document type"
463:     output: "Document type classification"
464:     validation: "Type must be one of: SKILL, Command, Knowledge, Spec, README"
465: 
466:   phase_2_template_selection:
467:     action: "Select appropriate template based on document type"
468:     output: "Template file path"
469:     depends_on: "phase_1_analysis"
470: 
471:   phase_3_population:
472:     action: "Populate template with user-provided content"
473:     output: "Draft document with filled sections"
474:     depends_on: "phase_2_template_selection"
475: 
476:   phase_4_validation:
477:     action: "Validate structure, frontmatter, section ordering"
478:     output: "Validation report (errors/warnings)"
479:     depends_on: "phase_3_population"
480: 
481:   phase_5_formatting:
482:     action: "Apply code standards (spacing, headers)"
483:     output: "Formatted document"
484:     depends_on: "phase_4_validation"
485: 
486:   phase_6_quality_check:
487:     action: "Review checklist + run AI quality evaluation"
488:     output: "Quality notes and improvement recommendations"
489:     depends_on: "phase_5_formatting"
490: ```
491: 
492: ### YAML Configuration: Feature Flags
493: 
494: **Before (Markdown Table)**:
495: ```markdown
496: | Feature           | Default | Description                         |
497: | ----------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
498: | strict_validation | true    | Enforce all validation rules        |
499: | auto_fix          | false   | Automatically fix formatting issues |
500: | frontmatter_check | true    | Validate frontmatter per document type |
501: ```
502: 
503: **After (YAML Configuration)**:
504: ```yaml
505: feature_flags:
506:   strict_validation:
507:     default: true
508:     description: "Enforce all validation rules without warnings"
509:     values: [true, false]
510: 
511:   auto_fix:
512:     default: false
513:     description: "Automatically fix formatting issues during validation"
514:     values: [true, false]
515:     warning: "Use with caution - may change document semantics"
516: 
517:   frontmatter_check:
518:     default: true
519:     description: "Validate frontmatter fields per document type"
520:     values: [true, false]
521:     enforcement_level: "error"
522: ```
523: 
524: ### YAML Workflow: Multi-Branch Decision Process
525: 
526: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
527: ```markdown
528: The system should detect when to generate variants:
529: - If user explicitly requests options (shows me options, variations, different approaches)
530: - If complexity is high (7+) and uncertainty signals are present (not sure, what would work)
531: - Otherwise, generate single solution
532: 
533: Variant count depends on complexity:
534: - Simple: 2-3 variants
535: - Standard: 3-5 variants
536: - Complex: 5-10 variants
537: ```
538: 
539: **After (YAML Multi-Branch)**:
540: ```yaml
541: variant_generation_logic:
542:   triggers:
543:     explicit:
544:       keywords: ["show me options", "variations", "different approaches", "multiple designs"]
545:       action: "Generate variants immediately"
546:       priority: "high"
547: 
548:     implicit:
549:       conditions:
550:         - "complexity >= 7"
551:         - "uncertainty_signals present"
552:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work", "best approach"]
553:       action: "Generate variants with uncertainty disclaimer"
554:       priority: "medium"
555: 
556:     default:
557:       action: "Generate single optimal solution"
558:       priority: "low"
559: 
560:   variant_count_guidelines:
561:     simple:
562:       complexity_range: [1, 3]
563:       variant_count: "2-3"
564: 
565:     standard:
566:       complexity_range: [4, 6]
567:       variant_count: "3-5"
568: 
569:     complex:
570:       complexity_range: [7, 10]
571:       variant_count: "5-10"
572: 
573:     user_specified:
574:       action: "Honor user's requested count"
575:       override: true
576: ```

578: ---
579: 
580: ## 8. CONFIGURATION TEMPLATES
581: 
582: **Purpose**: Demonstrate structured data formats for configuration and metadata.
583: 
584: ### YAML: Tool Configuration
585:

55: A skill README uses numbered ALL-CAPS H2 sections with `---` dividers between them. The default order:

57: | # | Section | Purpose | Keep When |
58: |---|---------|---------|-----------|
59: | 1 | AT A GLANCE | Four-row table a reader scans in five seconds | Always |
60: | 2 | OVERVIEW | What the skill is and what the reader gets first, then the optional problem narrative | Always (required by the validator) |
61: | 3 | QUICK START | The fastest path to a first result | Skill has commands, scripts or a workflow |

63: | 5 | INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION | When to use it, plus how it hands off to sibling skills | Readers can confuse it with a neighbor |
64: | 6 | TROUBLESHOOTING | The failure modes operators actually hit | Predictable issues exist |
65: | 7 | FAQ | The two to five questions readers keep asking | High-value answers exist |
66: | 8 | VERIFICATION | How you know the skill works | Skill ships a playbook or validation command |

13: 
14: # Skill README Template
15: 
16: Use this template for `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`. It writes a skill README in the same narrative voice the repo root `README.md` and the changelogs use: a one-line human pitch, an at-a-glance table near the top, a value-first overview, then quick start, navigation and a verification close.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: Give a person a fast, honest orientation to a skill before they open `SKILL.md`. The README answers what outcome the skill delivers, when to reach for it, what it does not own and how to navigate its files. `SKILL.md` stays the runtime instruction surface. The README is the front door a person reads.
25: 
26: ### Identity Guidance (Purpose First)
27: 
28: The identity of a skill is the outcome it delivers. State that outcome in one plain sentence before naming tools.
29: Describe CLIs, commands, routing paths and reference files only after the outcome.
30: A README that opens with a tool name has not stated its identity.
31: 
32: The mcp-obsidian README states the outcome first: it makes AI use inside Obsidian effective.
33: It names the CLIs and MCP server later as delivery surfaces.
34: Repeat the outcome in the frontmatter description and the pitch.
35: The description supports a quick scan. The pitch opens the full README.
36: 
37: ### Usage
38: 
39: Copy the fillable scaffold in Section 6 into `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`, then replace every placeholder with current behavior taken from the skill's real files. Keep the numbered ALL-CAPS section headers, the house style and the validator both require them. Drop any section that does not earn its place and renumber the rest.
40: 
41: ### Template Focus
42: 
43: The README gives people a human entry point, current capabilities and a clear route to supporting files. This template provides:
44: 
45: - A one-line pitch in a blockquote right after the H1, stating the outcome before any tool name.
46: - An identity guidance block that puts the delivered outcome ahead of the tooling.
47: - A capability section pattern for a skill's headline strengths, modeled on the pilot's Plugin Knowledge Layer.
48: - A dedicated HVR enforcement section with the banned forms and the scripted checks.
49: - Versioning conventions and a validation checklist that matches the pilot's gates.
50: 
51: ---
52: 
53: ## 2. SECTION MODEL
54: 
55: A skill README uses numbered ALL-CAPS H2 sections with `---` dividers between them. The default order:
56: 
57: | # | Section | Purpose | Keep When |
58: |---|---------|---------|-----------|
59: | 1 | AT A GLANCE | Four-row table a reader scans in five seconds | Always |
60: | 2 | OVERVIEW | What the skill is and what the reader gets first, then the optional problem narrative | Always (required by the validator) |
61: | 3 | QUICK START | The fastest path to a first result | Skill has commands, scripts or a workflow |
62: | 4 | HOW IT WORKS | The main workflow in prose, with a small Mermaid diagram for multi-step flows | Skill has non-obvious behavior worth explaining |
63: | 5 | INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION | When to use it, plus how it hands off to sibling skills | Readers can confuse it with a neighbor |
64: | 6 | TROUBLESHOOTING | The failure modes operators actually hit | Predictable issues exist |
65: | 7 | FAQ | The two to five questions readers keep asking | High-value answers exist |
66: | 8 | VERIFICATION | How you know the skill works | Skill ships a playbook or validation command |
67: | 9 | RELATED DOCUMENTS | Stable links out, `SKILL.md` first | Always when links exist |
68: 
69: `OVERVIEW` is the one required section. Its normalized name must appear as a numbered header so the validator finds it. Every other section is optional. A small utility skill might run four sections (AT A GLANCE, OVERVIEW, QUICK START, RELATED DOCUMENTS). A large orchestrator might run all nine. Match the count to the skill. Never pad to hit a number.
70: 
71: Inside OVERVIEW, start with `### What It Does`. Say what the skill is and what the reader gets.
72: Add up to two optional subsections after it.
73: Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to name a current reader problem.
74: Add the capability section below when it earns a table.
75: 
76: ### Capability Section Pattern
77: 
78: When a skill has a headline strength, add a named capability section after What It Does.
79: Use one or two short sentences to say why the strength matters.
80: Use an analogy only when it clarifies the mechanism.
81: Name the section after its domain and add one table row per capability.
82: State the file or data the skill can operate on.
83: Avoid marketing claims. The prose explains why the capability matters. The table states what it does.
84: 
85: ```markdown
86: ### The Plugin Knowledge Layer
87: 
88: | Plugin | What the skill knows how to operate |
89: |---|---|
90: | **Beancount Ledger** | append and patch balanced transactions in the structured `.beancount` ledger |
91: | **Obsidian Tables** | edit `columns`, `rows` and `views` inside `.table.md` JSON payloads |
92: ```
93: 
94: ---
95: 
96: ## 3. WRITING RULES
97: 
98: - Apply the [Prose Clarity Checklist](../../references/skill/creation-workflow.md#prose-clarity-checklist) to README prose.
99: - State the outcome before the tooling. The pitch and the identity guidance name what the reader gets. The tool names follow as the means.
100: - Open OVERVIEW with what the skill is and what the reader gets.
101: - Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to explain a current reader problem.
102: - Add a short context hook after the blockquote only when it helps the reader. Keep AT A GLANCE as the first numbered section.
103: - Carry the explanation in prose. Reach for a table only when 4 or more parallel items need a lookup grid (skill relationships, CLI flags, a comparison).
104: - Use semantic emoji only (✅ ❌ ⚠️ 🔒 🚨) for rules and status markers. Decorative section emoji never: that register belongs to the repository front-page README, while a skill README keeps the technical formatting.
105: - A short, concrete analogy can carry an abstract mechanism better than adjectives (the repo root README uses "like a lab notebook for software"). Use one only where it clarifies, never as decoration.
106: - Put the AT A GLANCE table first. Four rows, one line each, no prose cells.
107: - Name the canonical command or entry point in OVERVIEW or QUICK START so a reader knows where to start.
108: - Link to real files under `references/`, `assets/`, `scripts/`, `feature-catalog/` or `manual-testing-playbook/`. Verify each path resolves.
109: - State the expected output for every command you show, so a reader can tell success from failure.
110: - Be honest about boundaries and trade-offs. If the skill does not own something, say which skill does.
111: - Keep `SKILL.md` as the runtime surface. The README explains why and how to navigate. It does not restate long reference files.
112: - Follow the Human Voice Rules. Section 4 lists the banned forms and the scripted checks. It links the full ruleset.
113: - Vary subsection counts rather than defaulting to three.
114: - Document current behavior. Keep spec history out of the README.
115: - Use stable paths and commands. Update the README, its version and its changelog entry when behavior changes.
116: 
117: ---

119: ## 4. HVR ENFORCEMENT
120: 
121: Every README this template produces must pass the Human Voice Rules. The full ruleset lives at [`hvr-rules.md`](../../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
122: 
123: ### Banned Forms
124: 
125: The banned forms are: em dashes (U+2014), semicolons (U+003B), Oxford commas (a comma before the final and or or in a list), the hard-blocker words listed below and forced three-item groups.
126: 
127: ### Scripted Checks
128: 
129: Run the checks below from the skill root, with the README path as the argument. Each command must return zero matches. The punctuation checks use hex escapes on purpose: the commands stay clean of the characters they enforce.
130: 
131: ```bash
132: rg -n '\x{2014}' README.md
133: rg -n '\x{3B}' README.md
134: rg -n ',\s+(and|or)\b' README.md
135: rg -n '\b(delve|embark|realm|tapestry|illuminate|unveil|elucidate|abyss|revolutionise|game-changer|groundbreaking|cutting-edge|ever-evolving|shed light|dive deep|leverage|foster|nurture|resonate|empower|disrupt|curate|harness|elevate|robust|seamless|holistic|synergy|unpack|landscape|ecosystem|journey|paradigm|enlightening|esteemed|remarkable|skyrocket|skyrocketing|utilize|utilizing)\b' README.md
136: # Context-dependent words: landscape, ecosystem, journey, unlock, navigating
137: # Banned as metaphor, allowed in literal use. Judge each hit in context.
138: ```
139: 
140: The word check lists the hard blockers. A hit inside a code sample or a quoted command is exempt. A hit in prose is a violation. Context-dependent words from the full ruleset are banned as metaphor and allowed in literal use. Judge each hit in context.
141: 
142: Forced three-item groups are the fifth banned form. No exactly-three inline enumerations: use 2, 4 or 5 items. Tables and bullet lists are exempt. No exactly-three H3 subsections under every H2: vary the count.

146: ## 5. VERSIONING CONVENTIONS
147: 
148: Every skill README carries a version in its frontmatter: `version: X.Y.Z.W`, the same 4-part scheme `SKILL.md` uses. Bump the README version on every release, whether the change touched the README text or the skill it documents. The README states the current state, so a behavior change is a README change even when the prose barely moves.
149: 
150: Every release gets a per-skill changelog entry at `changelog/<version>.md`. The entry follows the shared [changelog template](../../../sk-create-changelog/assets/changelog-template.md) and its message-release shape: NEW covers what arrived, CHANGED covers what moved, NOT CHANGED covers what stayed untouched.
151: 
152: `SKILL.md` and the README carry versions that move together. A skill release bumps both files. The changelog entry records the new version.

13: # mcp-obsidian
14: 
15: > Obsidian is your knowledge base. This skill makes it an AI workspace too: notes, daily notes, tags and the data behind the plugins you rely on, all operable by an agent.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
20: 
21: | Aspect | What you get |
22: |---|---|
23: | **Use it for** | Note and vault operations in Obsidian, plus file-layer automation of the Health.md and Iconic plugins and the Obsidian theme system |
24: | **Invoke with** | "obsidian", "notesmd-cli", "obsidian vault", "daily note", "local rest api", a plugin name or an `obsidian_*` MCP operation |
25: | **Works on** | Vault files directly with no running app or through the live desktop app and its Local REST API when the situation needs it |
26: | **Produces** | Created, moved and tagged notes, daily notes, vault registrations, live-app opens and plugin data files edited at the file layer |
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ## 2. OVERVIEW
31: 
32: ### Why This Skill Exists
33: 
34: Obsidian holds your thinking. Notes, daily notes, tags and a stack of plugins that turn plain files into charts, dashboards and icon rules. The value of AI in that workspace comes from one thing: an agent that can actually work with what the vault contains.
35: 
36: That is the whole reason this skill exists. It makes AI use inside Obsidian effective. It knows how to read and write vault files headlessly, how to reach the live app when the UI itself is the goal and how to understand the plugins you run at the data level so it can operate them without guessing. The skill is not a launcher for two CLIs. The CLIs and the MCP are the means. Working with your knowledge and your plugins is the point.
37: 
38: ### What It Does
39: 
40: The skill gives an agent three ways to touch a vault, chosen by what the request needs:
41: 
42: - `notesmd-cli` (Yakitrak) operates the vault filesystem directly. No app, no token. Registration, search, print, create, move, delete, frontmatter, daily notes.
43: - The official `obsidian` CLI (ships with Obsidian desktop v1.12.4+) remote-controls an already-running app. It reaches what only the live app knows: the resolved link graph, the computed tag and task index, Bases, sync and file history, and plugin state.
44: - The cyanheads Obsidian MCP exposes a structured 12-tool `obsidian_*` surface through Code Mode when the live app and the Local REST API plugin are available. It is the specialist surface, not the default one.
45: 
46: On top of those surfaces sits the plugin knowledge layer. The mode treats each documented community plugin as a file format: Health.md export files with `health-viz` render blocks and the Iconic `data.json` rulebook. Alongside the plugins it operates the Obsidian theme system at the file layer: the theme package, `cssTheme` activation, CSS snippets and CSS variables. Instead of driving plugin UI that no headless agent can reach, it edits the data the plugin renders.
47: 
48: ### The Plugin Knowledge Layer
49: 
50: | Plugin | What the skill knows how to operate |
51: |---|---|
52: | **Health.md** | create and validate Apple and Android Health export files, place `health-viz` render blocks and detect the bundled mock-data fallback |
53: | **Iconic** | merge the canonical 21 file rules and 11 folder rules into `data.json` with backup-before-write discipline |
54: | **Theme system** | operate the Obsidian theme system at the file layer: activate a community theme via `cssTheme`, customize with CSS snippets and variables, and build or publish themes, never editing a shipped theme's own files (Minimal as the worked example) |
55: 
56: ---
57: 
58: ## 3. QUICK START
59: 
60: **Step 1: Install or inspect the headless profile.**
61: 
62: ```bash
63: bash .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/scripts/install.sh
64: ```
65: 
66: The script installs `notesmd-cli` through Homebrew when available, then prints the app-backed CLI and MCP setup steps without changing configuration files. Confirm with:
67: 
68: ```bash
69: notesmd-cli --version
70: notesmd-cli list-vaults
71: ```
72: 
73: `--version` prints a version string. `list-vaults` shows registered vaults and the default.
74: 
75: **Step 2: Register and confirm a vault.**
76: 
77: ```bash
78: notesmd-cli add-vault "/path/to/Vault"
79: notesmd-cli set-default-vault "Vault"
80: notesmd-cli list
81: notesmd-cli search "meeting"
82: ```
83: 
84: `notesmd-cli` now works without launching Obsidian. Empty `list` or `search` output is valid, not an error. It means the default vault is empty or has no match.
85: 
86: **Step 3: Enable the app-backed CLI only when the live UI is the target.**
87: 
88: In Obsidian desktop v1.12.4+: Settings → General → Command line interface → toggle on → Register CLI. That registers `obsidian` on PATH on macOS and Linux. Confirm it is usable with `obsidian version`, which exits 0 only when the binary is registered **and** the app is running, then read `obsidian help` for the command surface. The CLI does not launch Obsidian for you.
89: 
90: **Step 4: Use the MCP for structured live-app operations.**
91: 
92: The MCP needs a running Obsidian app, the Local REST API plugin v4.0.0+ with an API key and the `obsidian` Code Mode manual. Enumerate the tools before calling one:
93: 
94: ```typescript
95: const tools = await list_tools();
96: const info = await tool_info("obsidian.obsidian_get_note");
97: ```
98: 
99: ---
100: 
101: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
102: 
103: ### The Router
104: 
105: Every request starts with a surface decision. The headless filesystem path is the default because it works everywhere, even in CI and over SSH. When the work needs the running app, the official `obsidian` CLI is the default app-backed surface: it needs only the app, exposes 106 commands against the MCP server's 12, and answers in about 38 ms per call. The MCP server additionally needs the Local REST API plugin enabled, a bearer token and a Node process. Measured comparison: [`references/cli-versus-mcp.md`](./references/cli-versus-mcp.md).
106: 
107: | Need | Primary surface | Why |
108: |---|---|---|
109: | Vault registration, daily note, list, print, filename or content search | `notesmd-cli` | Filesystem-native and headless |
110: | Create, move, delete or edit frontmatter with no app | `notesmd-cli` | Works directly on vault Markdown files |
111: | Anything against a running app: read, write, search, link graph, tasks, Bases, sync, plugins, UI | official `obsidian` CLI | The default app-backed surface. 106 commands, app-only prerequisite, no server process |
112: | Section-scoped edits, tag-list management, JSON-typed frontmatter, or a batch over roughly 20 calls | `obsidian-mcp-server` via Code Mode | The only surface with in-place section patching and real tag lists, and the faster one once warm |
113: | Plugin data operations | file layer through either surface | The mode edits the files a plugin renders |
114: 
115: ### The File-Layer Doctrine
116: 
117: Obsidian plugins are render layers over plain data. The skill operates the data, not the UI. For each plugin it knows where the data lives, what shape it takes and how to mutate it safely. The full contract lives in `references/plugins/plugin-operation-logic.md`.
118: 
119: ### Safety Invariants
120: 
121: - Resolve the surface before acting. Do not launch Obsidian just to run a headless operation.
122: - Confirm the default vault before a write.
123: - Preview destructive note ops. Read a note before moving or deleting it.
124: - Quote note names and vault paths. They contain spaces.
125: - Treat empty search results as valid. Never invent a note.
126: - Confirm MCP tool names with `tool_info()` before calling `obsidian.obsidian_*`.
127: 
128: ---
129: 
130: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
131: 
132: ### When To Use This Skill
133: 
134: Use this mode for an Obsidian vault, a daily note, a note search, a Local REST API operation or one of the supported plugin data formats. Use `notesmd-cli` whenever a vault-file outcome is enough. When the running app is part of the result, use the official `obsidian` CLI. Escalate to the MCP server only for section-scoped editing, tag-list management or a long batch, and only after confirming the Local REST API plugin is enabled. The router prefers the headless path until a live-app capability is necessary, then the CLI until an MCP-only capability is.
135: 
136: ### Related Skills
137: 
138: | Skill | Relationship |
139: |---|---|
140: | `mcp-code-mode` | Owns the Code Mode MCP transport used by `obsidian.obsidian_*` calls |
141: | `mcp-click-up` | Structural sibling with the same CLI plus MCP orchestrator pattern |
142: | `sk-code` | Owns application-code standards when an application consumes or produces the notes |
143: 
144: ---
145: 
146: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
147: 
148: | What you see | Why | Fix |
149: |---|---|---|
150: | `notesmd-cli: command not found` | The headless CLI is missing or its install prefix is not on PATH | Run the mode-root installer and use its printed Scoop, AUR or source-build alternatives when Homebrew is unavailable |
151: | `notesmd-cli` has no default vault | No vault has been registered and selected | Run `notesmd-cli add-vault <path>` then `notesmd-cli set-default-vault <name>` |
152: | `obsidian: command not found` | The desktop CLI is not enabled or registered | In Obsidian v1.12.4+, enable Command line interface and click Register CLI |
153: | `The CLI is unable to find Obsidian` | Registered, but the Obsidian app is not running | Start Obsidian and wait for `obsidian version` to exit 0; the CLI will not launch it |
154: | MCP connection refused | The app is closed, Local REST API is disabled or the base URL is wrong | Start Obsidian with the target vault, enable Local REST API v4.0.0+ and check `OBSIDIAN_BASE_URL` |
155: | MCP returns 401 or 403 | `OBSIDIAN_API_KEY` is absent, wrong or the plugin is disabled | Copy a fresh Local REST API token into the Code Mode environment and restart the AI client |
156: | MCP tool not found | The manual is not registered or the callable name was guessed | Run `list_tools()` and `tool_info()`, then use `obsidian.obsidian_<tool>` after confirming it |
157: | Search returns no note | The query has no match or the wrong vault is active | Try `search-content`, check `list-vaults` and report the empty result if it stays empty |
158: 
159: Full recovery procedures live in `references/troubleshooting.md`.
160: 
161: ---
162: 
163: ## 7. FAQ
164: 
165: **Q: When should I use `notesmd-cli` instead of the official `obsidian` CLI?**
166: 
167: A: Use `notesmd-cli` for filesystem operations and any work that must run without the desktop app. Use the official CLI only for an app-backed outcome such as opening or controlling the live UI. They are different binaries with different runtime requirements.
168: 
169: **Q: When should I use the cyanheads MCP?**
170: 
171: A: For the four things the official CLI cannot do: patch a heading, block or frontmatter section in place, search and replace inside one note, add or remove a tag as a real YAML list, and set a JSON-typed frontmatter value. Also for a batch over roughly 20 calls, where a warm session costs 3 ms per call against the CLI's 38. For everything else against a running app, use the official CLI. Full evidence: [`references/cli-versus-mcp.md`](./references/cli-versus-mcp.md).
172: 
173: **Q: Does the install script change `.utcp_config.json` or `.env`?**
174: 
175: A: No. `scripts/install.sh` prints the exact Code Mode manual and `obsidian_OBSIDIAN_*` environment keys, and stays read-only. The `obsidian` manual and those keys are already registered in `.utcp_config.json` and `.env.example`; the installer never rewrites them.
176: 
177: **Q: How many MCP tools are there?**
178: 
179: A: Twelve are exposed. The server builds 14 and withholds `obsidian_list_commands` and `obsidian_execute_command` while `enableCommands` is false. All twelve are named and exercised in [`references/cli-versus-mcp.md`](./references/cli-versus-mcp.md). Confirm with `list_tools()` before relying on any signature.
180: 
181: **Q: Is an empty note search an error?**
182: 
183: A: No. Empty output means the selected vault has no match. Verify the vault and query spelling, then report the absence rather than creating a fictional result.
184: 
185: **Q: What does the skill know about my plugins?**
186: 
187: A: It ships reference sets for Health.md and Iconic, plus a general Obsidian theme-system reference set under `references/themes/`. Each set covers the data model, file-layer workflows and troubleshooting. The operation-logic reference generalizes the pattern to future plugins.
188: 
189: ---
190: 
191: ## 8. VERIFICATION
192: 
193: The mode-root scripts are the first checks because they separate required headless pieces from optional app-backed pieces.
194: 
195: | Check | How to run it |
196: |---|---|
197: | README structure | `python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/scripts/validate_document.py .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/README.md --type readme` reports zero issues |

201: | MCP health | With the manual registered, `list_tools()` shows `obsidian.obsidian_*` entries and `tool_info("obsidian.obsidian_get_note")` resolves a live schema |
202: | Example scripts | `mcp-roundtrip.sh` preflights and prints a Code Mode reference. Run `headless-notes-workflow.sh` only against a chosen vault |
203:

205:

117: Obsidian plugins are render layers over plain data. The skill operates the data, not the UI. For each plugin it knows where the data lives, what shape it takes and how to mutate it safely. The full contract lives in `references/plugins/plugin-operation-logic.md`.
118: 
119: ### Safety Invariants
120: 
121: - Resolve the surface before acting. Do not launch Obsidian just to run a headless operation.
122: - Confirm the default vault before a write.
123: - Preview destructive note ops. Read a note before moving or deleting it.
124: - Quote note names and vault paths. They contain spaces.
125: - Treat empty search results as valid. Never invent a note.
126: - Confirm MCP tool names with `tool_info()` before calling `obsidian.obsidian_*`.
127: 
128: ---
129: 
130: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
131: 
132: ### When To Use This Skill
133: 
134: Use this mode for an Obsidian vault, a daily note, a note search, a Local REST API operation or one of the supported plugin data formats. Use `notesmd-cli` whenever a vault-file outcome is enough. When the running app is part of the result, use the official `obsidian` CLI. Escalate to the MCP server only for section-scoped editing, tag-list management or a long batch, and only after confirming the Local REST API plugin is enabled. The router prefers the headless path until a live-app capability is necessary, then the CLI until an MCP-only capability is.

146: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
147: 
148: | What you see | Why | Fix |
149: |---|---|---|
150: | `notesmd-cli: command not found` | The headless CLI is missing or its install prefix is not on PATH | Run the mode-root installer and use its printed Scoop, AUR or source-build alternatives when Homebrew is unavailable |
151: | `notesmd-cli` has no default vault | No vault has been registered and selected | Run `notesmd-cli add-vault <path>` then `notesmd-cli set-default-vault <name>` |
152: | `obsidian: command not found` | The desktop CLI is not enabled or registered | In Obsidian v1.12.4+, enable Command line interface and click Register CLI |
153: | `The CLI is unable to find Obsidian` | Registered, but the Obsidian app is not running | Start Obsidian and wait for `obsidian version` to exit 0; the CLI will not launch it |
154: | MCP connection refused | The app is closed, Local REST API is disabled or the base URL is wrong | Start Obsidian with the target vault, enable Local REST API v4.0.0+ and check `OBSIDIAN_BASE_URL` |
155: | MCP returns 401 or 403 | `OBSIDIAN_API_KEY` is absent, wrong or the plugin is disabled | Copy a fresh Local REST API token into the Code Mode environment and restart the AI client |
156: | MCP tool not found | The manual is not registered or the callable name was guessed | Run `list_tools()` and `tool_info()`, then use `obsidian.obsidian_<tool>` after confirming it |
157: | Search returns no note | The query has no match or the wrong vault is active | Try `search-content`, check `list-vaults` and report the empty result if it stays empty |
158: 
159: Full recovery procedures live in `references/troubleshooting.md`.
160: 
161: ---
162: 
163: ## 7. FAQ
164: 
165: **Q: When should I use `notesmd-cli` instead of the official `obsidian` CLI?**
166: 
167: A: Use `notesmd-cli` for filesystem operations and any work that must run without the desktop app. Use the official CLI only for an app-backed outcome such as opening or controlling the live UI. They are different binaries with different runtime requirements.
168: 
169: **Q: When should I use the cyanheads MCP?**
170: 
171: A: For the four things the official CLI cannot do: patch a heading, block or frontmatter section in place, search and replace inside one note, add or remove a tag as a real YAML list, and set a JSON-typed frontmatter value. Also for a batch over roughly 20 calls, where a warm session costs 3 ms per call against the CLI's 38. For everything else against a running app, use the official CLI. Full evidence: [`references/cli-versus-mcp.md`](./references/cli-versus-mcp.md).
172: 
173: **Q: Does the install script change `.utcp_config.json` or `.env`?**
174: 
175: A: No. `scripts/install.sh` prints the exact Code Mode manual and `obsidian_OBSIDIAN_*` environment keys, and stays read-only. The `obsidian` manual and those keys are already registered in `.utcp_config.json` and `.env.example`; the installer never rewrites them.
176: 
177: **Q: How many MCP tools are there?**
178: 
179: A: Twelve are exposed. The server builds 14 and withholds `obsidian_list_commands` and `obsidian_execute_command` while `enableCommands` is false. All twelve are named and exercised in [`references/cli-versus-mcp.md`](./references/cli-versus-mcp.md). Confirm with `list_tools()` before relying on any signature.
180: 
181: **Q: Is an empty note search an error?**
182: 
183: A: No. Empty output means the selected vault has no match. Verify the vault and query spelling, then report the absence rather than creating a fictional result.
184: 
185: **Q: What does the skill know about my plugins?**
186: 
187: A: It ships reference sets for Health.md and Iconic, plus a general Obsidian theme-system reference set under `references/themes/`. Each set covers the data model, file-layer workflows and troubleshooting. The operation-logic reference generalizes the pattern to future plugins.

283: def discover_markdown_resources() -> set[str]:
284:     docs = []
285:     for base in RESOURCE_BASES:

289:     return {doc.relative_to(SKILL_ROOT).as_posix() for doc in docs}

291: def _guard_in_skill(relative_path: str) -> str:
292:     resolved = (SKILL_ROOT / relative_path).resolve()
293:     resolved.relative_to(SKILL_ROOT)
294:     if resolved.suffix.lower() != ".md":
295:         raise ValueError(f"Only markdown skill resources are routable: {relative_path}")
296:     return resolved.relative_to(SKILL_ROOT).as_posix()

298: def load_if_available(relative_path, loaded, seen, inventory) -> None:
299:     guarded = _guard_in_skill(relative_path)
300:     if guarded in inventory and guarded not in seen:
301:         load(guarded)

303:         seen.add(guarded)

305: def route_obsidian_resources(request: str) -> dict:
306:     """Score intent labels and load available Obsidian reference docs."""

311:     scores = {}

316:         )

323:         return {

325:             "needs_disambiguation": True,
326:             "disambiguation_checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST,
327:             "suggested_fallback": DEFAULT_RESOURCE,
328:             "resources": loaded,
329:         }
330: 
331:     # Error/install keywords boost TROUBLESHOOT/INSTALL regardless of other signals.
332:     if scores.get("TROUBLESHOOT", 0) > 3:
333:         intent = "TROUBLESHOOT"
334:     elif scores.get("INSTALL", 0) > 4:
335:         intent = "INSTALL"
336:     else:
337:         specific_plugin_intents = ("PLUGIN_ICONIC", "PLUGIN_HEALTH", "THEME_SYSTEM")
338:         matched_specific_plugin_intents = [
339:             plugin_intent
340:             for plugin_intent in specific_plugin_intents
341:             if scores.get(plugin_intent, 0) > 0
342:         ]
343:         if matched_specific_plugin_intents:
344:             max_specific_score = max(
345:                 scores[plugin_intent] for plugin_intent in matched_specific_plugin_intents
346:             )
347:             top_specific_plugin_intents = [
348:                 plugin_intent
349:                 for plugin_intent in matched_specific_plugin_intents
350:                 if scores[plugin_intent] == max_specific_score
351:             ]
352:             if len(top_specific_plugin_intents) > 1:
353:                 return {
354:                     "needs_disambiguation": True,
355:                     "candidate_intents": top_specific_plugin_intents,
356:                     "disambiguation_checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST,
357:                     "resources": loaded,
358:                 }
359:             intent = top_specific_plugin_intents[0]
360:         else:
361:             intent = max(scores, key=scores.get)
362: 
363:     for resource in RESOURCE_MAP[intent]:
364:         load_if_available(resource, loaded, seen, inventory)
365: 
366:     if not loaded:
367:         return {
368:             "load_level": "UNKNOWN_FALLBACK",
369:             "notice": f"No Obsidian reference docs available for intent '{intent}'",
370:             "disambiguation_checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST,
371:             "suggested_fallback": DEFAULT_RESOURCE,
372:             "resources": loaded,
373:         }

19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: An Obsidian vault or note request reaches this skill when it names Obsidian, a vault, `notesmd-cli`, the cyanheads MCP, the official app-backed `obsidian` CLI, or one of the two documented plugins, and the `mcp-tooling` hub's `mcp-obsidian` mode signal selects the packet. From there the router selects among the CLI command references, the official-CLI agent-usage guide, the cyanheads MCP tool catalog, the troubleshooting and Notion-migration guides, and the plugin and theme families under `references/plugins/` and `references/themes/`. `references/obsidian-cli-commands.md` is the declared default, offered as a fallback suggestion rather than loaded by any scored route.
24: 
25: The router answers one question: given a request, which skill-local resources load, in what order, and
26: what happens when nothing matches. Every path below stays inside this skill folder, and no resource
27: loads before an intent selects it.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. INTENT MODEL
32: 
33: Ten intents, one per `INTENT_SIGNALS` key. Each names the phrasing that fires it and the exact files its `RESOURCE_MAP` entry loads.
34:

36: - **`OFFICIAL_CLI`** — the app-backed official CLI: "official obsidian cli", "register cli", "obsidian version", "key=value", "backlinks", "orphans", "base:query", "file history" or "unable to find obsidian", loads `references/official-cli-agent-usage.md` and `references/obsidian-cli-commands.md`.

85: ### Two Decisions This Router Makes
86: 
87: 1. **CLI vs MCP** — filesystem/terminal work goes to a CLI; live-app note reads/writes/tags/search go to the MCP.
88: 2. **Which CLI profile** — headless `notesmd-cli` (default, no running app) vs the app-backed official `obsidian` CLI (a remote control for an already-running desktop app; it does not start one, and it exits 0 even on failure). Preflight and result-handling contract: `references/official-cli-agent-usage.md`.
89: 
90: ### Execution Profile Selection
91: 
92: | Surface | Binary / transport | Needs a running app? | Best for |
93: |---|---|---|---|
94: | **Headless CLI** | `notesmd-cli` (Bash) | No — operates on the vault filesystem | Daily note ops anywhere: open, daily, search, create, list, print, move, delete, frontmatter, vault management |
95: | **App-backed CLI** | `obsidian` (Bash) | Yes — the app must ALREADY be running; the CLI does not launch it | App-only outcomes: resolved link graph (`backlinks`/`orphans`/`unresolved`), computed tags and tasks, Bases queries, sync and file history, plugin/theme state, in-app opens |
96: | **MCP** | `obsidian.obsidian_*` via Code Mode | Yes — plus Local REST API + `OBSIDIAN_API_KEY` | Structured note reads/writes, tag management, semantic/global search over a live vault |
97: 
98: ```python
99: def resolve_execution_profile(request, runtime):
100:     """Pick the execution surface for an Obsidian operation.
101: 
102:     Best-effort runtime probes — never fabricated:
103:       runtime.app_running   -> an Obsidian desktop app is live
104:                                (probe: `obsidian version` prints a version number)
105:       runtime.rest_api_up   -> Local REST API plugin reachable on OBSIDIAN_BASE_URL
106:       runtime.api_key       -> OBSIDIAN_API_KEY present in the Code Mode environment
107:     """
108:     # MCP path needs a live app + Local REST API + token. It is the only surface
109:     # for structured note reads/writes, tag management and global/semantic search.
110:     if wants_structured_note_ops(request) and runtime.app_running \
111:             and runtime.rest_api_up and runtime.api_key:
112:         return "MCP"            # cyanheads obsidian-mcp-server via Code Mode
113: 
114:     # The official obsidian CLI is a remote control for an ALREADY-RUNNING app: it
115:     # does not launch one. Probe with `obsidian version` (exit 0 == registered AND
116:     # app up), then use it for app-only outcomes the filesystem cannot answer.
117:     # Its in-app failures exit 0, so callers must read stdout, not the status.
118:     if runtime.app_running and needs_app_command(request):
119:         return "OBSIDIAN_CLI"   # official `obsidian` CLI
120: 
121:     # Default: headless, filesystem-only, works with no running app or token.
122:     return "NOTESMD_CLI"        # Yakitrak notesmd-cli
123: ```

104: ### App-backed CLI — official `obsidian` (Live-App Path)
105: 
106: The official `obsidian` CLI shipped GA in Obsidian desktop **v1.12.4** (Feb 2026). It is a **remote control for an already-running app**, not a headless tool and not a launcher: with the app down it prints `The CLI is unable to find Obsidian` to stderr and exits 1. There is no npm/brew package — it ships with the desktop app.
107: 
108: **Enable in-app:** Settings → General → Command line interface → toggle on → "Register CLI" (auto-adds `obsidian` to PATH on macOS/Linux; on macOS this symlinks `/usr/local/bin/obsidian` into the app bundle).
109: 
110: **Syntax is `obsidian <command> key=value`,** with no POSIX flags: `obsidian version`, not `obsidian --version`. Use it for outcomes only the live app can produce — the resolved link graph, the computed tag and task index, Bases queries, sync and file history, plugin and theme state, and in-app opens.
111: 
112: **Two contracts before scripting it.** Run `obsidian version | grep -qE '^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+'` before you script. A version number means the CLI is registered and the app is running. Exit 0 alone does not, because a starting app can return 0 with an error.
113: Then stop trusting `$?`. Once the app is up, the CLI exits 0 even on failure and prints `Error: ...` to stdout.

265: | `obsidian append file="<name>" content="..."` | Append to a named note |
266: | `obsidian search query="..." format=json` | Search; JSON returns an array of paths |

268: | `obsidian property:set file="<n>" name=k value=v` | Set a frontmatter property |
269: | `obsidian backlinks file="<name>"` | Resolved backlinks — no filesystem equivalent |
270: | `obsidian tags` / `obsidian tasks` | The app's computed vault-wide index |
271: | `obsidian base:query file="<base>" format=json` | Query a Base |
